pages.title: Xin chào
pages.summary: Hello (universal greeting)

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: For travelers, Xin chào is the most dependable hello. It is polite, short, and safe when you walk into a shop, step up to a hotel desk, meet a guide, or start a simple request. In everyday Vietnamese, greetings often depend on age, gender, and relationship, so the next step is learning when to use chào plus a relationship word. If you are unsure, Xin chào lets you begin warmly without guessing the other person's role.

sections.title: Quick say
sections.body: Use Xin chào when you want one safe greeting. Use Chào when the moment is relaxed and the person already feels familiar.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: Xin gives the greeting a polite shape, chào carries the hello, and the full phrase is the safest default when you do not know the relationship word yet.

sections.title: Situational greetings
sections.body: Use these when the setting is more specific: a friend, a respectful adult, a phone call, or a time-of-day greeting.

sections.title: How locals actually greet
sections.body: This is the most local pattern. Pick the relationship word when the person's role is clear; stay with Xin chào when you are unsure. These words are not just family labels. In Vietnam they also show respect, age relationship, and social distance, which is why a greeting can sound warmer when the relationship word fits.

phrases.english: Hello, older brother / slightly older man
Hello, older sister / slightly older woman

sections.title: Common follow-ups
sections.body: After hello, small talk often checks health, movement, or the social moment. Use these when the exchange has room to continue.

sections.title: Cultural note
sections.body: Vietnamese greetings carry relationship information. Learning the pattern matters more than memorizing one perfect hello. You do not need to guess perfectly as a visitor; a calm Xin chào is accepted almost everywhere. As you get more comfortable, adding anh, chị, em, cô, chú, ông, or bà makes the greeting feel less like a phrasebook line and more like a real local opening.

A short thank-you keeps service moments warm and simple. Its job is giving the other person a simple anchor rather than a long explanation. The forms below show how tone, setting, or politeness changes the best choice.

pages.title: Dạ
pages.summary: Different ways to say Dạ in Vietnam start with hearing it as respect, not just yes.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Dạ is one of the most useful small words in Vietnamese. It can answer yes, show that you heard someone, soften the start of a sentence, or make a short reply sound respectful. Travelers should learn it as a polite response marker first, then choose Có, Không, Được, or Đúng when the answer itself needs to be clear.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Use Dạ when someone older, staff, a driver, or a local helper speaks to you and you want to answer politely before the main information.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: The whole word is short, so the useful lesson is what it does in the conversation.

breakdown.english: respectful yes / I hear you / softens the answer

sections.title: Answer choices
sections.body: Dạ can come before an answer, but these words carry the answer itself.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.body: Use it when a staff member asks a question, when an older person speaks first, when you are confirming that you heard instructions, or when you want to sound gentle before a short request. It works beautifully before Chào anh, Cảm ơn, or a yes/no answer.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: Dạ does not replace every yes. If the person needs a clear answer, say Dạ first if you want, then add Có, Không, Được, or Đúng.

sections.title: Explore next
sections.body: These are natural next steps after a polite acknowledgment.

pages.title: Đúng
pages.summary: Different ways to say Đúng in Vietnam focus on confirming that something is correct.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Đúng means yes in the sense of correct or right. Use it when someone checks a name, room number, pickup place, price, order, or direction and you want to confirm they have it right. It is different from Có, which often answers whether something exists or is available.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Say Đúng when the other person is checking a fact and you want a short confirmation.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: The word points to correctness, not just agreement.

breakdown.english: right / correct; yes, that is correct

sections.title: Nearby answers

sections.title: When to use it
sections.body: Use it when staff point to your booking name, a driver repeats the destination, a cashier confirms the item, or someone asks whether a detail is correct.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: For extra politeness, Dạ đúng is natural in many adult service moments, but Đúng by itself is still clear when the exchange is quick.

pages.title: Được

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Được is the compact okay when a plan works, a suggested option is acceptable, or someone asks whether something is possible. It is not just yes; it often means can, okay, allowed, or that works in context.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Use Được when you want to accept a practical option without adding a long sentence.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: Think of it as permission, possibility, and acceptance packed into one short word.

sections.title: Good to know

sections.body: Alô is the hello you use on the phone. It is useful for hotel calls, drivers, delivery, tour guides, and anyone calling to confirm a pickup or booking. It does not replace Xin chào in person; it belongs to the phone moment.

sections.title: The standard way

sections.title: Break it down

sections.title: Good to know

pages.title: Chào anh
pages.summary: A warm greeting for a slightly older man or adult male helper.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Chào anh is one of the most useful local-feeling greetings for travelers. Use it for a man who seems older than you, a driver, guide, shop worker, hotel staff member, or friendly helper when anh feels respectful and warm.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Say Chào anh when the person is male and older or socially senior enough that bạn would feel too flat.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: The relationship word carries the warmth.

sections.title: Relationship swaps

sections.title: When to use it
sections.body: Use it at a hotel desk, with a male driver, at a cafe counter, with a male guide, or with a man who is just a bit older than you. It is often warmer than Xin chào once the relationship is clear.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: Anh does not literally mean the person is your brother here. It marks age relationship and respect, which is why the greeting can sound more natural than a universal you.

pages.title: Chào bạn
pages.summary: A friendly neutral greeting for peers and warm casual help.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Chào bạn is the friendly version of hello when bạn fits the relationship. It works with peers, friendly helpers, classmates, younger adults near your age, or someone whose role feels casual rather than formal. If the person is clearly older or in a service role, Chào anh or Chào chị may sound warmer.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Use Chào bạn when you want a warm but simple hello and do not need to show extra age-based respect.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: The greeting is short, but bạn changes the relationship it creates.

sections.title: Natural variations

sections.title: When to use it
sections.body: Use it with a friendly guide, a peer at a class or tour, a casual local helper, or someone who has already made the exchange feel relaxed. In a formal service moment, start with Xin chào or Dạ, chào anh/chị.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: Bạn is useful, but it is not a perfect universal you. Vietnamese often prefers relationship words, so Chào bạn is best when you truly want a friendly neutral tone.

pages.title: Chào

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Chào is the plain greeting inside Xin chào. Use it when the moment is relaxed, the other person already feels socially clear, or you are adding a relationship word such as anh, chị, em, cô, or chú. If you are unsure, keep Xin chào as the safer first move.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Say Chào when a simple hi is enough. It is short and friendly, but it relies more on context than Xin chào.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: This is one word, but it becomes more useful when you notice what can come after it.

sections.body: Use Chào with people you already know, casual service moments where the mood is friendly, or as the base before a relationship word. Use Xin chào when you are entering a new shop, approaching a desk, or unsure how formal to be.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: Chào is not rude by itself; it is just lighter. Vietnamese often adds warmth through the word after Chào, so learning the relationship forms matters more than forcing one greeting everywhere.

sections.title: The standard way

sections.body: Use it before asking hotel staff for help, ordering at a counter, checking in with a guide, or starting a practical request with someone adult. It is especially useful when you do not want to guess the exact relationship word.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: Dạ adds a respectful shape without making the phrase long. It is a small word, but it can make the first line sound calmer and more locally aware.

sections.body: The last word turns the thank-you up a notch.

sections.title: Nearby thank-yous
sections.body: Choose the version that matches how much help you received.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.body: Use it after patient help, extra effort, a favor, a ride adjustment, a staff member checking something twice, or a local explaining something slowly.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: Nhiều makes the phrase warmer, but the short sentence still feels natural. A calm voice and a smile usually carry the gratitude better than adding more words.

pages.title: Không, cảm ơn
pages.summary: A polite refusal for vendors, offers, and small service choices.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Không, cảm ơn is the clean travel phrase for refusing without sounding abrupt. It is useful with vendors, extra bags, taxi offers, refills, menu suggestions, and anything you do not want but want to decline kindly.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Say Không, cảm ơn when the answer is no but you want the interaction to stay friendly.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: The thank-you softens the refusal.

sections.title: Nearby refusals
sections.body: Use these when the refusal needs more context.

phrases.vietnamese: Không, cảm ơn, tôi không quan tâm
phrases.english: No thank you, I’m not interested

phrases.english: No thank you, I’ll look around first
phrases.pronunciation: Khong cam on toi se xem xet xung quanh truoc

sections.title: When to use it
sections.body: Use it when declining a product, a ride, a refill, a table offer, a menu suggestion, or a street approach. Say it once clearly and keep moving if the moment is brief.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: The phrase is polite because it combines a clear no with gratitude. You do not need to explain unless the situation truly needs a reason.

sections.title: Explore next
sections.body: These help after a refusal or a simple polite exchange.

pages.title: Không có gì
pages.summary: A friendly reply when someone thanks you.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Không có gì is the reply to a thank-you: no problem, it is nothing, you are welcome. It is useful when a hotel worker, driver, classmate, or local thanks you for waiting, moving, paying, or being flexible.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Say Không có gì when you want to put the other person at ease after they thank you.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: The phrase literally says there is not anything to worry about.

sections.title: Thank-you pair
sections.body: This phrase answers gratitude; these are the lines it most often pairs with.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.body: Use it after someone thanks you for a small accommodation, apology, delay, or favor. It keeps the moment light and tells them there is no problem.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: Không có gì is a response, not the thank-you itself. If you are the one receiving help, start with Cảm ơn or Cảm ơn nhiều instead.

sections.title: Explore next
sections.body: These nearby pages help you choose the right polite reply.

pages.title: Anh khỏe không?
pages.summary: Different ways to say Anh khỏe không? in Vietnam use the older-man relationship word.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Anh khỏe không? is the warmer how are you for an older man, adult male helper, guide, driver, or staff member when the exchange has become friendly. It keeps the same pattern as Bạn khỏe không?, but anh makes the relationship clearer.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Use this after Dạ, chào anh or Chào anh when you have time for a friendly check-in.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: Only the first word changes from the peer version.

sections.title: Relationship forms
sections.body: Use the version that matches the person in front of you.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.body: Use it with an older male guide, driver, vendor, hotel worker, teacher, or local helper when you already greeted him and the mood has room for warmth.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: Anh can be respectful and friendly at the same time. If the man is clearly much older, chú or ông may fit better for greetings, but anh is common for many adult service moments.

sections.title: Explore next
sections.body: These phrases often sit next to this check-in.

pages.title: Bạn khỏe không?
pages.summary: Different ways to say Bạn khỏe không? in Vietnam start with choosing the right relationship word.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Bạn khỏe không? is the friendly peer version of how are you. It works after a greeting when the person feels close to your age, casual, or friendly enough for bạn. With older or younger people, Vietnamese often sounds warmer when you swap bạn for anh, chị, or em.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Use Bạn khỏe không? with peers, friendly guides, classmates, younger adults near your age, or someone who has already made the exchange casual.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: The pattern stays the same while the first word changes by relationship.

sections.title: Relationship forms
sections.body: Swap the first word when the person is clearly older or younger.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.body: Use it after Xin chào, Chào bạn, a first introduction, a class, a tour meetup, or a friendly repeated interaction. It is less natural as the very first sentence to a rushed stranger.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: In Vietnamese, the relationship word is part of the warmth. Getting bạn, anh, chị, or em close enough often matters more than adding extra words.

sections.title: Explore next
sections.body: After a friendly check-in, these keep the conversation easy.

phrases.pronunciation: zuht voo ee duhk gap ban

pages.title: Chị khỏe không?
pages.summary: Different ways to say Chị khỏe không? in Vietnam use the older-woman relationship word.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Chị khỏe không? is the friendly how are you for an older woman, adult female helper, guide, teacher, or staff member. It sounds more local than using bạn when the woman is clearly older or socially senior.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Use this after Dạ, chào chị or Chào chị when the greeting has opened into a friendly exchange.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: The question pattern is familiar; chị tells the listener who the question is for.

sections.title: Relationship forms
sections.body: Change the first word when the person changes.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.body: Use it with an older woman at a cafe, shop, hotel desk, class, tour, homestay, or local help moment when the exchange is warm enough for a check-in.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: Chị often lands warmly for a woman who is older than you but not aunt-age. For a clearly older woman, cô may fit better in greetings.

sections.title: Explore next
sections.body: These phrases often come before or after this check-in.

phrases.english: Respectful hello to an older woman

phrases.pronunciation: zuht voo ee duhk gap ban

pages.title: Em khỏe không?
pages.summary: Different ways to say Em khỏe không? in Vietnam use the younger-person relationship word.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Em khỏe không? is a friendly how are you for someone younger when the relationship is clear and relaxed. It can sound warm with a younger helper, student, younger staff member, or someone you have already greeted comfortably.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Use it when em is clearly appropriate and the check-in is friendly, not formal.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: Em changes who the question is aimed at while the health question stays the same.

sections.title: Relationship forms
sections.body: Use these when the person is a peer or older adult instead.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.body: Use it after Chào em or a friendly introduction when the person is younger and the moment has room for small conversation.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: Em can sound warm when the age relationship is clear. If you are unsure, Bạn khỏe không? is safer because it avoids choosing younger status for someone who may not expect it.

sections.title: Explore next
sections.body: These are useful nearby relationship phrases.

pages.title: Đi đâu đấy?
pages.summary: A friendly movement check that can follow a greeting.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Đi đâu đấy? literally asks where someone is going, but in friendly everyday speech it can work like light small talk after hello. Use it with someone familiar enough for a casual check-in, not as a serious route question to a rushed stranger.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Say Đi đâu đấy? when the conversation already has a friendly tone and the person is visibly heading somewhere.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: The phrase is short, but đấy makes it feel conversational.

sections.title: Natural greeting chain
sections.body: This line usually belongs after a greeting, not before one.

phrases.pronunciation: zuht voo ee duhk gap ban

sections.title: When to use it
sections.body: Use it with a familiar guide, classmate, host, neighbor, or friendly helper after you have already greeted each other. It fits best when the person is walking out, leaving the desk, or heading toward a visible next place.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: Because it can sound personal, keep it for friendly contexts. If you truly need directions from a stranger, ask a direction phrase instead.

sections.title: Explore next
sections.body: These pages help you choose between small talk and practical directions.

pages.title: Rất vui được gặp bạn
pages.pronunciation: zuht voo ee duhk gap ban
pages.summary: A warm first-meeting line after names or introductions.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Rất vui được gặp bạn is the friendly line for meeting someone for the first time. It works after names, introductions, a guide handoff, a class, a homestay welcome, or a helpful local exchange that becomes personal enough for warmth.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Say Rất vui được gặp bạn after the greeting and introduction, not as the first word at a counter.

phrases.pronunciation: zuht voo ee duhk gap ban

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: The sentence says you are very happy to get to meet the person.

sections.title: Natural introduction chain
sections.body: This line usually comes after a hello and before a thank-you or goodbye.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.body: Use it after someone introduces themselves, after meeting a guide or host, at a language exchange, in a class, or when a helpful local interaction turns into a friendly introduction.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: Bạn makes the phrase peer-friendly. With a clearly older person, the same idea can become more local when the relationship word changes, but this version is a safe first page for travelers.

sections.title: Explore next
sections.body: These help you start and close the same friendly exchange.

pages.title: Cảm ơn bạn đã hiểu
pages.summary: A warmer thank-you after a confusing or patient exchange.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.body: Cảm ơn bạn đã hiểu is for moments when the other person stayed patient while you explained, repeated, used translation, or corrected a misunderstanding. It thanks them for understanding, not just for a service.

sections.title: The standard way
sections.body: Say this after the problem is clear and the other person has accepted your explanation.

sections.title: Break it down
sections.body: The phrase adds the person and the reason for your thanks.

sections.title: Before this thank-you
sections.body: These are often the phrases that make this closing line useful.

phrases.vietnamese: Bạn có thể sử dụng những từ đơn giản hơn?
phrases.pronunciation: ban co the su dung nhung tu don gian hon

sections.title: When to use it
sections.body: Use it after a language mix-up, a patient explanation, a translated message, or a situation where the other person adjusted to your limited Vietnamese.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.body: This phrase is warmer than plain Cảm ơn because it names what you appreciate. It is a good closing line after a difficult interaction becomes cooperative.
